breaking.headline: Nvidia's $952 billion day: best since 2003
breaking.fact: Nvidia closed up 31.48% at $165.05 after the board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, adding roughly $952 billion in market value — the largest one-day gain ever for a U.S. company. The S&P 500 rose 4.73% and the Nasdaq 6.51%, their best days since April 2025.

breaking.headline: Gas falls to $3.64 ahead of Thanksgiving, down 18¢ in a week
breaking.fact: The national average for regular gasoline fell to $3.64 a gallon, its 29th straight daily decline and the lowest since March 13, as about 73 million Americans prepare to drive for Thanksgiving. AAA says the average could dip below the $3.58 Thanksgiving record set in 2022.

breaking.headline: Growth cools to a four-month low, but the economy is still expanding
breaking.fact: S&P Global's flash composite PMI eased to 54.6 in November from 55.9, with services at 54.7 and manufacturing at 54.5 — both still expanding. The survey still points to about 3% annualized GDP growth in the fourth quarter, though price gauges stayed well above the Fed's 2% target.

breaking.headline: Senate passes bipartisan energy permitting overhaul, 62–33
breaking.fact: The Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act on Thursday, speeding federal permits for power plants, pipelines, transmission lines and mines, and cutting the window to challenge projects from six years to 150 days. It also makes data centers pay for the grid upgrades they need. The bill now heads to the House.

watchlist.name: Air Liquide
watchlist.blurb: Air Liquide closed flat in Paris at €187.66, up 0.04% — $205.28 at the ECB's Nov 23 reference rate of 1.0939. The industrial-gas name sat out the U.S. rally entirely, its usual defensive profile on full display while tech soared. The 7-day sparkline in euros is a slow, orderly drift with no break in either direction. With no company news in play, the dollar price from here mostly tracks the euro.

watchlist.name: Anthropic
watchlist.blurb: Anthropic fell 1.43% to $87.64, the rare big name to miss today's rally as valuation doubts linger. The stock is still finding its level after Thursday's record debut — it opened at $111.50, closed day one at $97.17, then slid to $88.91 on Friday. Swings this wide are normal for a hot new listing with no trading history to anchor it. The $83 IPO price remains the line to watch underneath.

watchlist.name: SPDR 1-3 Month T-Bill ETF
watchlist.blurb: BIL ticked up 0.01% to $91.60, ballast on a day when almost everything else swung hard. The 1–3 month T-bill fund does exactly one job: it parks cash at a 4.04% distribution yield with essentially no price risk. Its latest distribution was $0.30849 a share, ex Nov 2 and paid Nov 5. On a day like today, this is the chip that lets the rest of the tape do whatever it wants.

watchlist.name: Alphabet
watchlist.blurb: Alphabet jumped 6.34% to $282.10, riding the AI rebound as the Huang news lifted the whole complex. Google's cloud and AI positioning put it among the day's outperformers, with Caterpillar the only Dow name ahead of it. The move recoups part of last week's rout but still leaves the stock below its recent highs. The test now is whether the rally holds once Wednesday's PCE report lands.

watchlist.name: Eli Lilly
watchlist.blurb: Eli Lilly rose 1.30% to $1,364.60, a solid but unremarkable gain on a day the market ripped higher. The drugmaker lagged the tech surge, as defensive health care often does when risk appetite returns all at once. Nothing company-specific drove the move; it simply rode the broad tape. Watch whether the stock reclaims its early-November levels if the rally extends into the holiday week.

watchlist.name: Cheniere Energy
watchlist.blurb: Cheniere inched up 0.21% to $295.46, barely moving while crude slid and natural gas fell sharply. The LNG exporter is caught between two forces: cheaper gas trims feedstock economics, while the Senate's permitting overhaul could speed new export terminals. Energy was the day's weak spot even as the broad market soared. The OPEC+ meeting on Sunday is the next catalyst for the whole complex.

watchlist.name: Nvidia
watchlist.blurb: Nvidia soared 31.48% to $165.05, its best day since May 2003, adding about $952 billion of market value — the largest one-day gain by a U.S. company. The board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO before the open, and the attorney general found no evidence he broke the law. The probes and investigation continue, with Huang testifying Dec 1. Sean's call stands: a long-term hold while all of that shakes out.

watchlist.name: Pfizer
watchlist.blurb: Pfizer finished flat at $27.40, the one chip on the tape that simply did not move. A Viagra-like pill from a rival showed promise against early Alzheimer's today, but that is another company's story, not Pfizer's. The stock's appeal remains its dividend and pipeline rather than any single day's tape. With the market roaring elsewhere, a flat close here is a reminder of how far health care lagged the rally.

watchlist.name: Rocket Lab
watchlist.blurb: Rocket Lab jumped 9.27% to $49.63, riding the risk-on wave as growth names snapped back. Space sentiment helped: SpaceX set a pad-turnaround record over the weekend with two Falcon 9 launches from one pad in 32 hours. Rocket Lab's own launch cadence remains the fundamental story underneath the tape. If the rally holds through Thanksgiving week, small-cap growth is where the beta lives.

watchlist.name: Rithm Capital
watchlist.blurb: Rithm Capital rose 1.37% to $8.16, joining the broad rally as financials caught a bid. The mortgage REIT's story is still the rate backdrop: the 10-year held near 4.92% and markets price a December Fed hike at roughly 90%. Its dividend remains the draw for income holders. Watch Wednesday's PCE report — a hot print would push hike odds higher and test the whole rate-sensitive complex.

watchlist.name: SPAC Index ETF
watchlist.blurb: The SPAC index fund climbed 4.35% to $133.35, swept along by the broadest rally in months. Blank-check names are pure risk appetite, and today had it in abundance after the Huang news removed a systemic worry. The fund still sits well below its autumn highs after last week's rout. Whether this is a durable turn or a one-day squeeze depends on what Wednesday's inflation data says.

watchlist.name: Truist Financial
watchlist.blurb: Truist rose 2.36% to $46.89 as banks joined the rally, with financials among the day's steadier gainers. The regional bank benefits when the yield curve and credit sentiment both cooperate, and today delivered both. Nothing bank-specific drove the move; it was the tape. The Senate's permitting bill, if it clears the House, could eventually lift loan demand for energy and infrastructure projects.

watchlist.name: United States Antimony
watchlist.blurb: U.S. Antimony surged 7.17% to $2.39, and the bottom watch fired at the close — the oversold bounce the watch was built for. The stock is up off its recent lows as the whole risk complex snapped back. Antimony's strategic-mineral story still hinges on China export curbs and U.S. defense demand, neither of which changed today. The question now is whether the bounce holds or fades into the holiday week.

watchlist.name: Uranium Energy Corp
watchlist.blurb: Uranium Energy jumped 10.19% to $5.84, off Friday's $5.30 low, and the bottom watch fired at the close. The move tracks the broad risk rebound, but uranium has its own tailwind: the Senate's permitting overhaul would speed approvals for mines and nuclear projects. UEC remains a favorite on valuation and balance sheet. A hold above $5.50 into the holiday week would confirm the low is in.

watchlist.name: Valero Energy
watchlist.blurb: Valero fell 1.43% to $329.40, one of the day's few decliners as crude slid 4.4% to $80.25 a barrel. Refiners felt the squeeze from both sides: cheaper crude and falling gasoline prices ahead of Thanksgiving. Energy was the weak spot on a day the broad market soared. Sunday's OPEC+ meeting is the next swing factor for the whole oil complex, with the group weighing output against the surplus.

watchlist.name: Vanguard Target Retirement 2035
watchlist.blurb: The target-date fund's NAV slipped 2.08% to $27.75, a rare down day that runs against the equity rally. Target-date NAVs can gap on year-end distributions, so the December statement will tell the tale — the fund's equity sleeve could not have lost 2% on a day the S&P rose 4.7%. For now, treat the print as an accounting artifact rather than a market call. The long-run glide path is unchanged.

watchlist.name: Vanguard Institutional 500 Index Trust
watchlist.blurb: The S&P-anchored estimate rides the index's surge: $148.76 (est.), up 4.73%. It is built from the Nov 3 anchor — $155.58 when the S&P 500 closed 7,568.92 — and it has tracked the fund closely: Friday's actual close printed $142.17 against a $142.04 estimate. Days like today are the anchor's best case, since the estimate is the index. When the real NAV prints, expect it within a few dimes of this figure.

watchlist.name: Schwab Value Advantage Money Fund
watchlist.blurb: Schwab's money fund holds its stable $1.00 NAV with a 7-day SEC yield of 3.77%, as published Nov 20. It is the sweep vehicle, where idle Schwab cash sits between CD purchases, and the plan is to sell it down whenever any account tops $1,000. Its yield trails the Treasury-only funds because it holds a broader mix. The comparison rate is VUSXX's 4.03% — the standing argument for keeping sweep balances small.

watchlist.name: Vanguard Treasury Money Market Fund
watchlist.blurb: Vanguard's Treasury money fund holds $1.00 with a 7-day SEC yield of 4.03% as published Nov 20 — still the best yield in the cash class on this tape. Treasury-only holdings keep it as close to risk-free as a fund gets, and the 0.07% expense ratio leaves almost nothing on the table. It out-yields Schwab's sweep by about a quarter point. Every CD on the ladder has to beat this rate to earn its place.

weekInBrief.headline: Japan's Nikkei drops 5% as the AI selloff spreads in Asia
weekInBrief.body: Japan's Nikkei fell 5% on Monday, its second sharp drop in two sessions, as the AI-led selloff that hammered Wall Street last week spread across Asia. The contrast with New York could not have been starker: while Tokyo slid, U.S. stocks staged one of their best days in years on the Huang news.

weekInBrief.headline: Gold and silver snap back after last week's slump
weekInBrief.body: Gold bounced 4.45% to $3,671.90 and silver jumped 5.73% to $43.58 on Monday, snapping back as margin pressure eased and the panic hedging of last week unwound. Both metals remain well below their autumn highs after a brutal week, but the rebound tracked the broader risk rally.

weekInBrief.headline: Black Friday: 182.7 million Americans expected to shop
weekInBrief.body: The National Retail Federation expects 182.7 million consumers to shop over the five days from Thanksgiving to Cyber Monday. Oxford Economics expects holiday retail sales to grow 4.2%, or 2.2% after inflation — though higher gasoline, energy and food prices are squeezing household budgets.

weekInBrief.headline: Bitcoin bounces from weekend lows near $55,000
weekInBrief.body: Bitcoin climbed back above $61,000 on Monday after plunging to about $55,130 over the weekend amid $2.4 billion in crypto liquidations. The bounce tracked the broader liquidity rebound as Nvidia's return removed a systemic worry, though the coin remains far below its recent highs.

items.headline: Latest from the Strait
items.body: U.S. Central Command denied as “FALSE” Iran's claim that its air defenses struck and damaged a U.S. F-16 over the Gulf on Saturday, saying all U.S. fighter jets in the region are safe and accounted for. President Trump said Sunday he is inclined to resume major strikes against Iran after the new year if negotiations fail, while Iran's foreign minister said nuclear talks can only begin as a “second stage” after the strait reopens. The Joint Maritime Information Center's Nov. 22 assessment warned further attacks near the Omani side of the strait are “highly likely.” On the oil itself, UANI satellite imagery — corroborated by Windward — caught the first ship-to-ship transfer of Iranian crude since July: about 200,000 barrels moved from the sanctioned tanker Olym to the Hao Fan on Nov. 17, though the receiving tanker's whereabouts are now unknown and no Iranian cargo has been confirmed through the strait; Kpler still puts the non-Iranian oil flowing through at roughly 9.5 to 10 million barrels a day, about a quarter below October's pace.

space.headline: SpaceX sets pad-turnaround record: two launches from one pad in 32 hours
space.body: A Falcon 9 carrying classified National Reconnaissance Office satellites lifted off from Vandenberg's SLC-4E on Sunday, just over 32 hours after a Space Force mission left the same pad — a new record for the fastest turnaround at a single launch pad. The booster, B1097, completed its 14th flight and landed back at Vandenberg. Two more Vandenberg launches are lined up for Tuesday and Saturday.

space.headline: A Viagra-like pill may slow early Alzheimer's, trial finds
space.body: A year-long trial of AR1001 — a pill already sold in South Korea for erectile dysfunction — found it slowed cognitive decline by 31% in the 604 patients with early Alzheimer's who were not taking other dementia drugs. The effect vanished when the full 1,500-patient group was counted, so experts call the result promising but early. The findings were presented Nov. 16 at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease conference.

space.headline: One supergene decides whether a moss ant queen flies or stays put
space.body: Harvard and University of Georgia researchers found a single supergene — a 6.5-million-base-pair stretch of chromosome 1 — that decides whether a developing moss ant queen grows wings or emerges wingless, with worker-like traits mixed in. One copy is enough: the variant is dominant. The work, in Science Advances, shows how a new caste can evolve by tweaking an existing developmental program.

space.headline: Bacteria split their own membranes to stop viruses spreading
space.body: Chinese Academy of Sciences researchers uncovered a new bacterial immune trick: after a phage infection, a signaling molecule called 2′,3′-cGAMP drives a protein to split the bacterium's membrane into two bilayers, killing the infected cell before the virus can spread. The study, in Molecular Cell, also found the T4 phage fights back with a protein that mops up the signal. It is a previously unknown branch of the CBASS antiviral system.

apod.title: Outbursts from a Massive Star
apod.credit: NASA/CXC/Univ. of Virginia/M. Aghakhanloo et al.; Optical: SDSS
apod.explanation: Using NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory, astronomers have discovered what is triggering repeated outbursts from a giant, unstable star in the galaxy NGC 4559, about 30 million light-years away. The star, AT 2016blu, is at least 33 times the Sun's mass — and a hidden companion, either a black hole or a neutron star, pulls material from it every 113 days, heating the stolen gas until it shines in X-rays.
